questions.stem: The Shakhty trial of 1928, in which mining engineers were accused of sabotage, is significant because it:
options: began a campaign against 'bourgeois specialists' as the Five-Year Plan began
ended the purges of the party and led to the release of political prisoners
was the first trial of leading Old Bolsheviks such as Zinoviev and Kamenev
showed that the courts could acquit defendants who resisted the regime
questions.explanation: The engineers were convicted of 'wrecking' in a show trial. It signalled that failures in industry would be blamed on class enemies and saboteurs, a pattern repeated through the 1930s. The trials of Old Bolsheviks came in 1936-38.

questions.stem: Magnitogorsk, built from 1929 in the southern Urals, is best known as:
options: the site of the largest Gulag camp for political prisoners
the city where Stalin's forces stopped the German advance in 1942
a model collective farm shown to foreign visitors in the 1930s
a giant new steel-making city that symbolised the Five-Year Plans
questions.explanation: Magnitogorsk was built almost from nothing around a huge iron and steel works, by volunteers, peasants fleeing the villages and forced labourers. It showed both the enthusiasm and the hardship of Stalin's industrialisation.

questions.stem: Historian Stephen Kotkin's study of Magnitogorsk argued that its people learned to 'speak Bolshevik'. He meant that:
options: citizens learned the regime's language and values and used them for their own ends
the government forced all non-Russian workers to learn Russian before getting jobs
workers secretly rejected socialism while publicly praising Stalin at every meeting
the party banned all languages except Russian in the new industrial cities
questions.explanation: Kotkin, a post-revisionist, argued Stalinism was a civilisation people took part in, adopting its identities to advance or protect themselves. This differs from views stressing either pure terror from above or hidden resistance.

questions.stem: The Soviet Constitution of 1936, often called the 'Stalin Constitution', is best described as:
options: creating a multi-party parliament with free elections and an independent press
giving the republics the right to leave the Soviet Union and form their own states
transferring power from the Communist Party to the trade unions and soviets
promising wide rights and equal suffrage on paper while the Great Terror began
questions.explanation: The constitution guaranteed freedoms of speech and assembly, and ended the class-based voting restrictions of earlier constitutions, but the party's monopoly remained. It was proclaimed as mass arrests were beginning, a sharp contrast between words and practice.

questions.stem: In 1938 Nikolai Yezhov was replaced as head of the NKVD by Lavrentiy Beria. What did this change signal?
options: the abolition of the secret police and the closing of the Gulag
Stalin's loss of control over the security forces to the army
the winding down of the mass terror; Yezhov was later shot
the beginning of the Great Terror and the first show trials
questions.explanation: The worst of the terror, often called the Yezhovshchina, ended in late 1938. Yezhov was arrested in 1939 and executed in 1940, a sign that even its organisers could become victims. The Gulag continued to grow.

questions.stem: Robert Conquest's The Great Terror (1968) is associated with the view that:
options: the purges were driven mainly by local officials, with Stalin reacting to events
the number of victims of the purges was much smaller than Western writers claimed
the purges were a necessary response to real plots by German and Japanese spies
Stalin personally directed the purges, which killed very large numbers
questions.explanation: Conquest's work, based on the sources then available, stressed Stalin's central role and very high death tolls. Revisionists such as J. Arch Getty emphasised chaos and pressures from below. Archival research after 1991 confirmed Stalin's direct involvement in key decisions.

questions.stem: The Winter War of 1939-40 between the Soviet Union and Finland:
options: exposed Red Army weaknesses, though Finland ceded land in the peace
ended in a Soviet defeat and the loss of Leningrad to Finnish forces
led Britain and France to declare war on the Soviet Union in 1940
was won quickly by the Red Army within the first two weeks of fighting
questions.explanation: Finland resisted far longer and more effectively than expected, inflicting heavy losses. The USSR gained land, including the Karelian Isthmus, in March 1940 and was expelled from the League of Nations. The poor performance encouraged Hitler to underestimate the Red Army.

questions.stem: In 1940 the Soviet secret police shot about 22,000 Polish officers and other prisoners at Katyn and other sites. How did the Soviet government treat the massacre for almost fifty years?
options: It admitted responsibility in 1945 and paid compensation to the families
It denied the killings ever took place and banned all research on Poland
It said the prisoners had been killed fighting in the Red Army against Germany
It blamed Nazi Germany and admitted Soviet responsibility only in 1990
questions.explanation: When Germany announced the discovery of graves in 1943, Moscow blamed the Nazis, and this remained the official line until Gorbachev's government acknowledged NKVD responsibility in 1990. Katyn shows how the regime controlled the history of the war.

questions.stem: In June 1940, as Germany defeated France, the Soviet Union:
options: occupied Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania and made them Soviet republics
invaded Finland for the first time and captured its capital, Helsinki
declared war on Germany in support of France and Britain
handed eastern Poland back to an independent Polish government
questions.explanation: Under the secret protocol of the Nazi-Soviet Pact the USSR occupied the Baltic states and took Bessarabia from Romania. Arrests and mass deportations of 'anti-Soviet elements' followed, shaping these nations' memory of Soviet rule.

questions.stem: A labour decree of June 1940 shows the regime preparing the Soviet home front for war. It:
options: allowed workers to elect factory managers in defence industries
abolished internal passports so workers could move freely to new jobs
made lateness and changing jobs without permission criminal offences
reduced the working week to five days to raise workers' morale
questions.explanation: The decree lengthened the working day and tied workers to their jobs, with prison terms for repeated absence. Such laws were enforced harshly during the war. Internal passports had been introduced in 1932 to control movement.

questions.stem: Soviet citizens called the war against Germany from 1941 to 1945 the:
options: War of the Peoples
Great Patriotic War
Great Fatherland Struggle
Second Civil War
questions.explanation: The name echoed the 'Patriotic War' against Napoleon in 1812, stressing national defence rather than communist revolution. It became central to Soviet and later Russian identity, marked by Victory Day on 9 May.

questions.stem: Soon after the German invasion, the State Defence Committee was set up in June 1941. Its significance was that it:
options: ran the evacuation of Moscow after Stalin and the government left the city
concentrated political, economic and military power under Stalin
took control of the war away from Stalin and gave it to a council of generals
was elected by the Supreme Soviet to negotiate peace terms with Germany
questions.explanation: The committee, chaired by Stalin, directed the entire war effort. Stalin also became people's commissar of defence and supreme commander. Stalin stayed in Moscow during the German advance in late 1941.

questions.stem: In his radio broadcast of 3 July 1941, Stalin addressed Soviet citizens as 'brothers and sisters' and called for:
options: an immediate armistice with Germany to save Soviet cities
a general retreat to Siberia and the abandonment of Moscow
a workers' uprising in Germany against Hitler's government
a scorched-earth policy and partisan war behind the lines
questions.explanation: Stalin's unusually personal appeal urged that nothing useful be left to the enemy and that partisan units be formed. The tone marked a shift to patriotic language that would continue through the war.

questions.stem: In 1941-42 more than a thousand factories were moved east, to the Urals, Central Asia and Siberia. This evacuation is significant because it:
options: left the Red Army without tanks or aircraft until American supplies arrived in 1944
was ordered by Germany as part of the terms of a temporary armistice in 1941
moved factories into areas already captured by the German army in the east
allowed Soviet war production to recover and overtake Germany's in key weapons
questions.explanation: Whole plants and their workers were moved by rail and rebuilt, sometimes producing again within weeks. By 1943 the USSR was outproducing Germany in tanks and aircraft, a key factor in victory.

questions.stem: Order No. 227 of July 1942, known as 'Not one step back!', ordered that:
options: troops must not retreat without orders, with blocking units behind them
all Soviet prisoners of war must be exchanged for German prisoners at once
civilians in Stalingrad be evacuated across the Volga before the battle began
officers be elected by their soldiers to improve morale in the Red Army
questions.explanation: Issued as German forces advanced towards Stalingrad and the Caucasus, the order created penal battalions and blocking detachments. It shows the coercion that accompanied patriotism in the Soviet war effort.

questions.stem: During the war Stalin restored Russian military heroes such as Alexander Nevsky and Kutuzov as national symbols, and in 1943 dissolved the Comintern. What do these changes suggest?
options: Stalin had given up communism and planned to restore the monarchy after the war
the party had lost control of propaganda to the army and the Orthodox Church
the Soviet Union was preparing to make a separate peace with Nazi Germany
Russian patriotism and alliance needs outweighed revolutionary ideology
questions.explanation: Orders named after Nevsky, Suvorov and Kutuzov rallied soldiers through national pride, and dissolving the Comintern reassured Britain and the USA. These were pragmatic shifts; the party's control remained.

questions.stem: In September 1943 Stalin met leaders of the Russian Orthodox Church, and a new patriarch was soon elected. The main reason was to:
options: return all church property seized since 1917 to the Orthodox clergy
persuade the Pope to condemn the German invasion of the Soviet Union
win popular support for the war and improve the USSR's image with its allies
end the separation of Church and state and make Orthodoxy the state religion
questions.explanation: The Church had supported the war effort since 1941, and Stalin allowed it to reopen churches and seminaries under state supervision. Religion was tolerated as long as it served the state.

questions.stem: During the siege of Leningrad (1941-44), the 'Road of Life' was:
options: a radio program that broadcast news of victories to the starving city
the route across frozen Lake Ladoga for supplies and evacuees
a railway built by German prisoners to connect Leningrad with Moscow
the main street of Leningrad, defended by workers' militias to the end
questions.explanation: Lorries crossed the ice of Lake Ladoga in winter, and boats in summer, under German fire. The siege lasted about 872 days and huge numbers of civilians died, mostly of starvation and cold.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of Soviet women in the Great Patriotic War?
options: Women were conscripted into combat roles in equal numbers with men from 1941
Most women left paid work to care for children evacuated to the east
Hundreds of thousands served in the forces, and women did much of the farm and factory work
Women were excluded from all military roles and sent to work on collective farms only
questions.explanation: Soviet women served as snipers, pilots, such as the 'Night Witches' bomber regiment, medics and anti-aircraft gunners. On the home front they made up a large majority of collective farm workers and a large share of industrial labour.

questions.stem: In 1943 and 1944 entire peoples, including the Chechens, Ingush, Kalmyks and Crimean Tatars, were:
options: granted independence for fighting bravely against the Germans
conscripted into special units that led the assault on Berlin
deported to Central Asia and Siberia for alleged collaboration
evacuated to the Urals to protect them from German occupation
questions.explanation: The NKVD deported whole nationalities in brutal conditions, and many died in transit or exile. The Volga Germans had been deported in 1941. Most were allowed to return only after Stalin's death, and the Crimean Tatars much later.

questions.stem: How did the Soviet state treat many of its soldiers who returned from German prisoner-of-war camps in 1945?
options: They were welcomed as heroes and given land and pensions on their return
They were allowed to settle in the West if they chose not to go home
They were made officers in the occupation forces in eastern Germany
They were screened by the NKVD, and many punished as suspected traitors
questions.explanation: Millions of Soviet prisoners had died in German captivity. Survivors went through filtration camps; some were sent to the Gulag or labour battalions, as surrender had been treated as treason since 1941.

questions.stem: German occupation policy in Ukraine and other Soviet lands after 1941 helped the Soviet war effort, despite some initial welcome for the invaders in places. The best explanation is that:
options: Germany handed the occupied regions to Romanian and Finnish rule from 1941
the occupied population was evacuated by Germany to work on farms in France
Nazi racial policy brought mass killing, hunger and forced labour, causing hostility
German forces gave land back to peasants, which made Soviet partisans unnecessary
questions.explanation: Some peasants hoped the Germans would end collective farms, but Nazi policy treated Slavs as inferior: Jews were murdered, food was seized and millions were deported for labour. Brutality drove recruits to the partisans.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the importance of Lend-Lease aid to the Soviet war effort?
options: It provided most of the tanks used at Stalingrad and Kursk, without which the USSR would have lost
It was refused by Stalin, who would not accept help from capitalist countries
It began only after Germany surrendered, so it had no effect on the fighting
It supplied trucks, food and materials that aided mobility, though Soviet output did most
questions.explanation: American trucks, rail equipment, food and raw materials were especially valuable from 1943, helping the Red Army's advances. Soviet historians long played down its role; most weapons used by the Red Army were Soviet-made.

questions.stem: At the Tehran Conference of November-December 1943, Stalin's main achievement was:
options: the admission of the Soviet Union to the League of Nations as a permanent member
a promise that the United States would share the secret of the atomic bomb
a firm Anglo-American commitment to open a second front in France in 1944
an agreement that Germany would be divided into two states after the war
questions.explanation: Stalin had long demanded a second front to relieve pressure on the Red Army. At Tehran, Roosevelt and Churchill committed to the landings that took place in Normandy in June 1944.

questions.stem: The Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945 and then:
options: invaded Japanese-held Manchuria
landed troops on the island of Honshu
bombed Tokyo with long-range aircraft
signed a peace treaty with Japan at once
questions.explanation: Stalin had promised at Yalta to enter the Pacific war within three months of Germany's defeat. The Red Army attacked Manchuria on 9 August 1945, the day of the Nagasaki bomb, and later occupied northern Korea.

questions.stem: In April-May 1945 the Red Army under commanders including Zhukov and Konev:
options: captured Vienna and Prague but was ordered by Stalin not to enter Germany
liberated Paris together with Free French forces under de Gaulle
captured Berlin, where Hitler killed himself before Germany's surrender
halted on the Oder River while British and American troops took Berlin
questions.explanation: The Battle of Berlin cost both sides heavy losses. Hitler died on 30 April, and the German surrender was signed on 8 May, celebrated in the USSR on 9 May as Victory Day.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the war strengthened Stalin's regime rather than weakening it?
options: Victory gave the system and Stalin new legitimacy, and the USSR emerged as a superpower
The war forced Stalin to share power with elected soviets, which made the regime popular
The Soviet Union suffered few losses, so living standards rose sharply after 1945
Stalin's generals took over the party after 1945 and introduced democratic reforms
questions.explanation: Despite enormous losses, victory over Nazi Germany became the regime's greatest source of pride, and Soviet power now reached into Eastern Europe. Hopes for post-war relaxation were disappointed as repression resumed.

questions.stem: Historian Richard Overy, in Russia's War (1997), argued that the Soviet system contributed to victory. Which evidence best supports this view?
options: Stalin's purges removed many experienced officers from the Red Army in 1937-38
Stalin ignored repeated warnings of a German attack in the first half of 1941
Millions of Soviet soldiers were encircled and captured in the first months of the war
Central planning moved industry east and outproduced Germany in key weapons by 1943
questions.explanation: Overy stressed how the Soviet state mobilised labour and resources and how the Red Army learned and reformed. The other options are evidence that Stalinism weakened the USSR's readiness, the opposing case.

questions.stem: In his 'Secret Speech' of 1956, Khrushchev criticised Stalin's war leadership. A historian using this speech as evidence should note that:
options: Khrushchev had opposed Stalin openly throughout the 1930s and 1940s
Khrushchev had political reasons to blame Stalin and distance himself
Khrushchev had no access to official records and relied only on rumours
the speech was written by Western historians and published under his name
questions.explanation: Khrushchev attacked Stalin's cult of personality and errors such as ignoring warnings in 1941, partly to strengthen his own position. He had served loyally under Stalin, so the speech is valuable but needs to be read for its purpose.

questions.stem: Soviet war deaths, military and civilian, were the highest of any country in the Second World War. For a study of the national experience, this is most significant because:
options: it shows that the Red Army was defeated in most battles after 1943
it proves that the German army suffered few losses on the Eastern Front
it led the Soviet Union to disarm completely after the war ended
the scale of loss shaped Soviet society and memory for decades
questions.explanation: Losses in the tens of millions left a severe shortage of men, millions of orphans and devastated regions. The memory of sacrifice became central to Soviet identity and to its post-war demand for security in Eastern Europe.
